metadata.notes: Framework dictionary for TLCTC v2.6 — the single normative authority for cluster definitions, axioms, and classification rules; all TLCTC documents declare which version of this dictionary they implement. Per-cluster boundary tests are normative but homed in the core paper (§4) by design; this dictionary deliberately carries no boundary_tests field. Lineage: v2.3 consolidated finalized v2.1 content (transit, intra-system, and unresolved-step extensions) with no new normative content vs v2.1. v2.3.1 erratum (2026-07-01): a single axiom-conformance correction — #4 Identity Theft generic_vulnerability retightened from lifecycle/credential-protection wording to the point-of-authentication binding gap, so the field no longer claims scope that R-CRED and Axioms VI/VII/X assign to enabling clusters (storage/transmission/acquisition). Cluster identity and IDs unchanged. v2.3.2 erratum (2026-07-26): a single axiom-conformance correction — #5 Man in the Middle generic_vulnerability retightened from "lack of sufficient control, integrity protection, or confidentiality over the communication channel/path" to "The lack of sufficient control over the communication path", removing consequence-side (confidentiality/integrity) and control-side vocabulary from a cause-side field per Axioms III and V. Cluster identity, IDs, definition, attacker's view, topology, and boundary tests unchanged. v2.4 (2026-07-28): a single clarifying, backward-compatible change on the interaction model — Axiom II restated to remove the network precondition ("All networked systems" → "All system interactions, networked or intra-system"), and R-ROLE extended to state that roles are established by call direction at any interface, including intra-system privilege interfaces (syscall, hypercall, IPC, driver IOCTL), with a cross-reference to R-INTRA-7 so the boundary crossing is not misread as a classification input. No cluster identity, ID, definition, attacker's view, generic_vulnerability, or topology changed; the axiom set is unchanged in count and numbering; no rule was added or removed. Classifications valid under v2.3.2 remain valid under v2.4 — the change resolves an ambiguity rather than altering a decision. Vertical stack analysis (whitepaper §13.5) remains applied guidance and is deliberately NOT part of this dictionary: it introduces no generic vulnerability, axiom, or disambiguation rule and is derivable from Axiom II + R-ROLE + R-INTRA-7 over the 'intra-privilege' boundary context. v2.5 (2026-08-07): two disambiguation rules added — R-CHANNEL and R-SUBSTRATE — completing the family begun by R-FLOOD. Each resolves a weakness describable either as a specific generic vulnerability or as a generic code defect in favour of the specific one, leaving R-ROLE as the residual test. R-CHANNEL: where the defective logic is constitutive of a communication-path control (peer authenticity, channel encryption, algorithm negotiation), the cluster is #5, not #2/#3; R-ROLE governs only where the defect is incidental to the control. R-SUBSTRATE: #8 requires a physical-layer property of the substrate to be the exploited generic vulnerability, and where the physical layer is only the readout channel for a defect in implemented logic the cluster is #2/#3 — attacker proximity or possession is explicitly NOT the test. Rule count 16 → 18; the two are recorded as complementary to the legacy R-PHYSICAL (admission versus sequencing). UNLIKE v2.4, this release is NOT classification-preserving: both rules alter decisions that were defensible under v2.4, and the CWE mapping was re-adjudicated accordingly (certificate/peer-authenticity family → #5; the #8 bucket re-audited from 81 entries to 16, with the remainder resolving to #2, #2 | #3, #2 | #8 or #1 on the property test). No cluster identity, ID, generic_vulnerability, or topology changed; the axiom set is unchanged in count and numbering. Records classified under 2.4 SHOULD be re-checked against R-CHANNEL and R-SUBSTRATE; tlctc-framework.v2.4.json is retained unchanged so those records keep a stable reference. v2.5 pre-publication consistency pass (2026-08-08): #2 and #3 definition and attackers_view retightened from "source code implementation" wording to "implementation flaws within a component acting in a server/client role", making the substrate-neutrality already established by R-ROLE and R-SUBSTRATE explicit in the definitions themselves — implementation flaws in firmware, microcode, or hardware logic classify by component role, resolving the hardware-substrate open question recorded in the CWE mapping notes. Generic_vulnerability fields (already substrate-neutral: "Server-/Client-side implementation flaws enable unintended behavior") unchanged; cluster identity, IDs, and topology unchanged. Rule registry clarified as exactly these 18 rules; v2.0 whitepaper rule IDs R-ABUSE, R-HUMAN, and R-PHYSICAL are retired aliases whose substance is carried by the cluster definitions and boundary tests, and a retired ID is never reused with a different meaning. v2.5 R-CRED clarification (2026-08-14): a single normative clarification to R-CRED (self-issued identity), part of the in-progress v2.5 editing version prior to the first v2.5 Zenodo deposit — v2.5 content, not a post-release erratum. R-CRED's #4 assignment now carries the proviso that credential application is #4 only where the identity claimed is not the presenter's own: a credential issued to the presenter by the target system through a designed enrolment function makes the presenter its authentic holder, so authentication as self exploits no #4 binding gap; where the enrolment function granted the identity or its permissions outside their intended population or scope, that enrolment step maps to #1. This makes explicit in the rule registry the scope the #4 generic_vulnerability already implies ('the authentic holder of the identity it claims') and closes a gap in which an attacker holding a self-enrolled principal was read as #4 by analogy to unauthorized account use. Companion boundary tests added to the core paper §4 (#1 and #4). No cluster identity, ID, definition, attacker's view, generic_vulnerability, or topology changed; the axiom set and rule count (18) are unchanged. UNLIKE the v2.4 clarification, this change is NOT fully classification-preserving: records that classified use of a self-enrolled account as #4 SHOULD be re-checked against the proviso; it joins the v2.5 delta (with R-CHANNEL, R-SUBSTRATE, and the #2/#3 retightening). The canonical-authority declaration was additionally tightened to state that per-cluster boundary tests are normative and homed in the core paper (§4). v2.5 DRE refinement tree (2026-09-05): a new optional data_risk_events section records the Data Risk Event type codes as a refinement tree — C; I with Ii (incorrect state: correspondence/completeness fails) and If (misattributed state: provenance/attribution fails); A with Av (unavailable state) and Ac (inaccessible state) — together with the stopping rule that admits exactly these two splits: a property is split only where the resulting states are distinguishable by inspecting the record itself, never by the story of how it got there. Av/Ac were already v2.5 prose and grammar; Ii/If are new, and they replace the '[DRE: Im]' (manipulated) code proposed for v2.6 in the OpenAI–HF AP-7 path, which fails the stopping rule by naming the actor's intent rather than a record state. Classification-preserving: a parent code stays legal whenever the refinement is unknown or irrelevant, so every existing [DRE: I] and [DRE: A] remains correct; the Layer 3 schema enum and both ABNF grammars now carry all seven codes. No cluster identity, ID, definition, attacker's view, generic_vulnerability, or topology changed; the axiom set and rule count (18) are unchanged. Part of the in-progress v2.5 editing version prior to the first v2.5 Zenodo deposit. v2.5 scope rule and SRE types (2026-09-05): R-SCOPE added to the registry (rule count 18 -> 19; nine core rules, ten v2.1 extension rules) — a step is classified under a cluster only where the action fell outside the entitlement envelope an accountable grantor conferred for it; an intended in-grant action is Abuse of Rights, operational risk, no cluster, no SRE. New optional cause_side_partition section (three questions, four rows — failure, error in use, abuse of rights, attack — entitlement definitions, third-party modifier, decision procedure) and new optional system_risk_event section widening the SRE to two types at one altitude: Compromise (loss of control, an actor holds capability, reached only through cluster steps, the cyber pivot) and Failure (loss of function, no actor). No cluster identity, ID, definition, attacker's view, generic_vulnerability, or topology changed; the axiom set is unchanged. Classification-preserving for Attack-row records; records that classified an entitled actor's in-grant action as #1 SHOULD be re-checked against R-SCOPE. v2.5 SRE re-centering and #8 retightening (2026-09-10): (1) #8 Physical Attack definition retightened from "hardware, facilities, media, interfaces, or signals" to "hardware, media, interfaces, or signals" - the cluster is about hardware and OT reached physically, and a facility is the envelope through which hardware is reached, not the thing compromised; attacker's view, generic_vulnerability ("physical accessibility of infrastructure"), ID and topology unchanged. (2) system_risk_event re-centered: the SRE the framework defines is System Compromise alone; System Failure moves from `types` to a new `other_system_altitude_events` block as its standing example, so that the text agrees with the figures (which draw Compromise alone) and the clusters' pivot is not presented as one of two co-equal types; the schema cardinality of `types` moves 2 -> 1 and admits the new block. (3) The definition now states that every cluster step records an SRE (a path of n cluster steps records n, each admitting a DRE, a chained SRE, or both), which the core paper, glossary and application paper had already adopted. (4) Core paper section 6 rule-count wording corrected ("eighteen" -> nineteen); the registry itself was already 19. Classification-preserving throughout: no step classified under v2.5 changes cluster. Rule count 19 unchanged; axiom set unchanged. v2.6 (2026-09-22, working version - not deposited, not deployed): answers an external review with nineteen change items recorded in changes_from_v2_5. R-FLOOD, R-CHANNEL and R-SUBSTRATE are folded into R-SPECIFIC (registry 19 -> 17; the three IDs are retired aliases with their v2.5 meaning); the #10 definition names subversion, with a subversion test (a flaw in a legitimately supplied component is classified where it is exploited) and federation read as #4 unless the identity provider was subverted; the entitlement envelope is scope (objects, actions, limits) and purpose is the conduct norm; R-SCOPE step 4 routes to the cluster rules; a new fec section carries the data-vs-code boundary and the prompt-injection position; System Compromise is restated around behaviour leaving owner control, and only steps that succeeded are classified. NOT classification-preserving: records that classified a flaw in a legitimately supplied third-party component as #10, or a service provider's acceptance of a non-subverted identity provider's assertion as #10, SHOULD be re-checked; tlctc-framework.v2.5.json is retained unchanged. Boundary tests remain homed in the core paper (section 4) and are now mirrored into whitepaper section 4.1 under a build check.

#1.name: Abuse of Functions
#1.definition: An attacker abuses the logic or scope of existing, legitimate software functions for malicious purposes without exploiting a code flaw.
#1.attackers_view: I abuse a functionality, not a coding issue.
#1.generic_vulnerability: The inherent trust, scope, and complexity designed into software functionality and configuration.

#2.name: Exploiting Server
#2.definition: An attacker targets implementation flaws within a component acting in a server role.
#2.attackers_view: I abuse an implementation flaw in a component acting in a server role.
#2.generic_vulnerability: Server-side implementation flaws enable unintended behavior.

#3.name: Exploiting Client
#3.definition: An attacker targets implementation flaws within any component acting in a client role.
#3.attackers_view: I abuse an implementation flaw in a component acting in a client role.
#3.generic_vulnerability: Client-side implementation flaws enable unintended behavior.

#4.name: Identity Theft
#4.definition: An attacker misuses authentication credentials to impersonate an identity.
#4.attackers_view: I abuse stolen or forged credentials to act as someone else.
#4.generic_vulnerability: Insufficient binding, at the point of authentication, between a presented credential and the authentic holder of the identity it claims.

#5.name: Man in the Middle
#5.definition: An attacker intercepts, modifies, or relays communication between two parties by exploiting a privileged position on the communication path.
#5.attackers_view: I abuse my position between communicating parties.
#5.generic_vulnerability: The lack of sufficient control over the communication path.

#6.name: Flooding Attack
#6.definition: An attacker intentionally overwhelms system resources or exceeds capacity limits through a high volume of requests, data, or operations, leading to denial of service.
#6.attackers_view: I abuse the circumstance of always limited capacity.
#6.generic_vulnerability: Finite capacity limitations inherent in any system component.

#7.name: Malware
#7.definition: An attacker abuses the inherent ability of a software environment to execute foreign executable content, including malicious code or legitimate tools executing attacker-controlled code.
#7.attackers_view: I abuse the environment's designed capability to execute malware code, malicious scripts, or foreign-introduced tools for my purposes.
#7.generic_vulnerability: The software environment's designed capability to execute potentially untrusted foreign code.

#8.name: Physical Attack
#8.definition: Unauthorized physical interaction with or interference to hardware, media, interfaces, or signals—via direct contact or exploitation of physical phenomena/emanations.
#8.attackers_view: I abuse the physical accessibility or properties of hardware, devices, and signals.
#8.generic_vulnerability: Physical accessibility of infrastructure and the exploitability of physical-layer properties.

#9.name: Social Engineering
#9.definition: An attacker psychologically manipulates individuals into performing actions counter to their best interests.
#9.attackers_view: I abuse human trust and psychology.
#9.generic_vulnerability: Humans can be influenced into unsafe actions or decisions.

#10.name: Supply Chain Attack
#10.definition: An attacker compromises systems by subverting third-party software, hardware, services, or update mechanisms that the target trusts and integrates, so that the subverted artifact is accepted as authoritative inside the target's domain.
#10.attackers_view: I abuse the trust in third-party components.
#10.generic_vulnerability: Trust in third-party components and update channels can be subverted.

axioms.statement: The framework is generic and applies to all IT systems; it does not differentiate by system type.
All system interactions, networked or intra-system, can be abstracted as client-server interaction.
axioms.notes: v2.4 clarification: a network is not a precondition. A syscall, hypercall, or IPC call establishes the same caller-called relation as a remote protocol exchange, so intra-system privilege interfaces are inside the interaction model. Prior wording ('All networked systems') was read by some implementers as excluding them.

axioms.statement: Threats are on the cause side; outcomes and events are not threats.
Threat clusters are separate from threat actors.
For every generic vulnerability, there is one threat cluster (non-overlap).
Each distinct attack vector is defined by the generic vulnerability it initially targets.
Top-level clusters have sub-threats (strategic vs operational layering).
Clusters can be used in sequence to describe an attack path; Δt measures velocity.
Credentials are system control elements; acquisition and application are distinct steps.

rules.statement: If Foreign Executable Content executes, a #7 step MUST be recorded at the execution moment.

Classify by the role of the component containing the flaw relative to the attacker: server-role flaw = #2, client-role flaw = #3. Roles are established by call direction at any interface, including intra-system privilege interfaces (syscall, hypercall, IPC, driver IOCTL); a network is not a precondition.
rules.notes: v2.4 clarification. A kernel handling a crafted syscall from a lower-privileged process is in server-role for that interaction (#2); a higher-privileged component consuming data or responses returned from a lower-privileged one is in client-role (#3). Per R-INTRA-7 the boundary crossing itself remains an observability annotation and MUST NOT be treated as a classification input — the cluster follows from the role at the interface, exactly as it does across a network.

rules.statement: Where one weakness is describable both as a specific generic vulnerability and as a residual one, classify it under the specific. The residual tests — designed functionality (#1) and implementation flaw (#2/#3 per R-ROLE) — apply only where no specific generic vulnerability is the one exploited. Three clauses decide the recurring cases: (capacity) if the primary mechanism is volume or intensity exhausting finite resources, #6; an implementation defect causing crash, hang or degradation is #2/#3; (channel) if the defective logic is itself a communication-path control — peer authenticity (certificate validation, chain of trust, hostname matching, expiry or revocation checking), channel encryption, or algorithm negotiation — #5; a defect incidental to that control is #2/#3; (substrate) if a physical-layer property of the substrate — charge, voltage, electromagnetic emission, temperature, emission-borne timing, wear, or material state — is itself the exploited generic vulnerability, #8, whether or not the attacker has physical access; where the physical layer is only the readout channel for a defect in implemented logic, classify by that defect.
rules.notes: v2.6 consolidation (C2). Folds the v2.5 rules R-FLOOD (capacity), R-CHANNEL (channel) and R-SUBSTRATE (substrate) into one rule; each clause reproduces the retired rule's proposition unchanged, and the retired IDs remain aliases of their clauses with their v2.5 meaning (an ID is never reused). The rule states the derivation principle the three instantiated: the residual clusters — #1 for designed functionality, #2/#3 for implementation flaws — apply only where no specific generic vulnerability is the one exploited. Channel: the test is constitutive versus incidental, not server versus client — a missing or incorrect certificate check IS the absence of control over the communication path, while memory corruption in a TLS parser remains #2/#3; the clause classifies the weakness, R-MITM sequences the path. Substrate: the question is whether the attack is against the implemented logic or against the physical representation it runs on — Rowhammer is #8 (charge migration is the vulnerability, mountable from JavaScript, which is why proximity is not the test), Spectre is #2 (speculation crosses a designed isolation boundary; timing is only the readout), power analysis is #8 (the cryptography is correct; the emission is the vulnerability); the location of a flaw — hardware, firmware, silicon — never determines the cluster, and where foreign code executes to induce the effect the execution is a separate #7 step (#7 -> #8). The substrate clause is the admission test for #8; the sequencing principle once stated as R-PHYSICAL (a retired v2.0 alias) still holds. R-CRED and R-EXEC apply the same principle to #4 and #7 but also split one action into two steps, so they remain separate rules.

rules.statement: #10 Supply Chain Attack MUST be placed at the Trust Acceptance Event (TAE) — the moment the third-party trust link is honored and the trust artifact becomes authoritative inside the target domain. A #10 step requires that the trust artifact, or the third party issuing it, was subverted before acceptance; a defect in a legitimately supplied component is classified where it is exploited.
Position acquisition maps to the enabling cluster; once position is established, interception/modification/relay actions map to #5.

Credential acquisition maps to the enabling cluster. Credential application (use of the credential to authenticate) is ALWAYS classified as #4 Identity Theft, regardless of the acquisition method, PROVIDED the identity claimed is not the presenter's own. A credential issued to the presenter by the target system through a designed enrolment function makes the presenter its authentic holder; such use MUST NOT be classified as #4, and where the enrolment function granted the identity or its permissions outside their intended population or scope, the enrolment step maps to #1. These are separate attack steps.
rules.notes: v2.5 clarification (self-issued identity). Makes normative in the rule registry what the #4 generic_vulnerability already implies ('the authentic holder of the identity it claims'): when the target system itself issued the credential to the presenter, the point-of-authentication binding between presented credential and authentic holder is intact, so authentication as self exploits no #4 generic vulnerability — the exploited generic vulnerability is the scope of the enrolment function and of the permissions attached to the resulting principal (#1). Examples (non-normative): fictitious or pseudonymous self-registration is #1, no identity being impersonated; enrolment completed AS an existing identity (e.g. domain-based auto-affiliation, or identity verification satisfied via prior access to the victim's mailbox) is #1 -> #4 — the enrolment abuse is #1, the subsequent authentication as the victim is #4. NOT fully classification-preserving: records that classified use of a self-enrolled account as #4 SHOULD be re-checked.

rules.statement: A step is classified under a cluster only where the action fell outside the entitlement envelope an accountable grantor actually conferred for it. Cause-side classification asks three questions in strict order: (1) Is there an actor? No: failure or external event — operational risk, no cluster. (2) Did the actor intend the outcome? No: Error in Use — operational risk, no cluster. (3) Did an accountable grantor confer an entitlement covering THIS action? Yes: Abuse of Rights — operational risk, no cluster, no System Risk Event; the consequence chain starts at the Data Risk Event. Otherwise the step is an attack and is classified under the cluster rules — for example #2 or #3 per R-ROLE where an implementation flaw was required, #1 Abuse of Functions where a designed function was used outside the envelope — cyber, SRE recorded. Entitlement means entitled, not permitted: its envelope is scope (objects, actions, limits), purpose is the conduct norm, and it attaches to the person, not the token — use of a credential by anyone other than its grantee is never inside an envelope (#4 per R-CRED, subsequent function use #1), and exploiting an implementation flaw is never inside any grant.
rules.notes: v2.5 scope rule (2026-09-05). Makes explicit in the registry the scope boundary the framework has always asserted: cyber risk addresses unauthorized or unknown entities, and an entitled actor inside their grant is neither. It is NOT an actor test (Axiom IV): the question is a relation between the action and the conferred envelope, never who the actor is — an outsider with no grant and an insider acting outside their grant land in the same Attack row and the same cluster. 'Insider threat' is therefore not a TLCTC category; it is a mixture of two rows answering to two control regimes. Abuse of Rights is not an eleventh cluster because it has no generic vulnerability: #1's exposure (the designed scope of functionality) is reducible by design, whereas a granted entitlement is irreducible by design — remove it and you have removed the business, not secured the system. Rights are functions (every authorization check is designed functionality), which is why the two abuses look alike; rights are the subset of functions that partitions the invocation of all the others, and the taxonomy turns on which side of that partition the action fell, never on which function was called or who called it. Entitlement is tested after intent and before any cluster test because an entitled actor exploiting a code flaw is an attack. Companion definitions live in the cause_side_partition section; worked cases (support agent, database administrator, claims handler, self-enrolment, stolen credentials) in the core paper section 3.5. Classification-preserving for Attack-row records; records that classified an entitled actor's in-grant action as #1 SHOULD be re-checked.

rules.statement: Vendor code running on the target device is NOT transit. Software executing on the victim's own device is the attack surface, classified by R-ROLE (typically #3), not a transit (relay/carrier) party.
Intra-system boundary crossings never change cluster classification. They are observability annotations, not classification inputs.
The 'memory' intra-system boundary type is deferred and MUST NOT be used.
'?' and '…' are epistemic annotations, NOT clusters. They have no generic vulnerability, do not appear in cluster definitions, and must not be referenced as if they were '#11'/'#12'.
'?'/'…' are excluded from statistics — they represent absence of knowledge, not a category.
DRE tags ('+ [DRE: ...]') MUST NOT be appended to '?'/'…'. Without a classified cluster there is no causal basis for asserting a data risk event in the notation.
Boundary operators ('||...||', '⇒', '|...|') MAY appear adjacent to '?'/'…' — boundaries are independently observable.
Every '?'/'…' is an open analytical task. Progressively replace with classified steps as evidence matures.
Any path containing '?'/'…' MUST carry a prose annotation explaining what is unresolved and why.
Binary rule: if any cluster can be defended — even weakly — use '#X [conf=low]', not '?'. Reserve '?'/'…' for genuine 'we know something happened, we don't know what' situations.

fec.definition: Foreign Executable Content (FEC): attacker-controlled or otherwise untrusted program content that a general-purpose execution engine in the target environment loads, interprets, or executes through its designed execution capability. Its execution is the generic vulnerability of #7 Malware and triggers R-EXEC. There is no on-disk requirement: in-memory, interpreted, macro and reflectively loaded content is FEC.
fec.boundary: Domain-specific expression languages are data, not FEC, unless they cause execution in a general-purpose engine. Injection that only reads or writes data is #2/#3 without #7 (SQL injection reading a table: #2). Where the injected expression reaches a general-purpose engine the execution is FEC and a #7 step follows (SQL injection invoking xp_cmdshell or COPY ... PROGRAM, server-side template injection reaching a code-evaluation call: #2 -> #7). Natural-language instructions to a model or agent are not FEC: acting on natural-language input is the model's designed function (prompt injection is #1); code or commands the agent then executes whose content the attacker controls are FEC (#1 -> #7).
fec.notes: v2.6 (C10, C11). Consolidates into the dictionary the normative Data vs Code Boundary that the v2.0 whitepaper (Execution Terms) and the glossary already stated, and which the CWE mapping already applied (CWE-89 SQL injection #2; CWE-77/78 command injection #2 -> #7). The #7 scope wording 'attacker-controlled commands fed into interpreters' is narrowed to general-purpose interpreters accordingly. The prompt-injection position is the one the MITRE ATLAS mapping and the agentic attack paths already apply.

data_risk_events.description: Data Risk Event (DRE) type codes used in '+ [DRE: ...]' tags. Three parent properties — C (Confidentiality), I (Integrity), A (Availability/Accessibility) — with two admitted refinements: I → Ii/If and A → Av/Ac. A parent code stays legal whenever the refinement is unknown or irrelevant. Codes are outcome annotations recorded on the record that changed state: never clusters, never classification inputs (Axiom III), and never appended to unresolved steps (R-UNRES-5).
data_risk_events.stopping_rule: Split a property only where the resulting states are distinguishable by inspecting the record itself — never by the story of how it got there. The rule admits exactly two splits (I → Ii/If: check provenance and attribution; A → Av/Ac: is the data absent, or present and unusable?), refuses every split of C (accidental versus deliberate disclosure is provenance; one party versus public is extent, i.e. severity, not a state), and refuses any split by cause — outcomes never inherit the classification of the step that produced them (Axiom III).

codes.name: Loss of Confidentiality
codes.definition: Data has been disclosed to a party not entitled to it. No refinement: disclosed data is disclosed, and the record's standing is identical however it leaked.

codes.name: Loss of Integrity
codes.definition: The standing of a record as a faithful and attributable representation has changed other than through its intended, authorised process. Use I when it is unknown or irrelevant whether correspondence (Ii) or provenance (If) failed.

codes.name: Incorrect state
codes.definition: The record no longer corresponds to what it represents, or is no longer complete; read off the record, the content is wrong. Answered by validation, reconciliation and four-eyes controls.

codes.name: Misattributed state
codes.definition: The record claims an origin, author or authority it does not have; read off the record, provenance fails while the content may be perfectly accurate. Answered by segregation of duties, provenance logging and behavioural monitoring.

codes.name: Loss of Availability / Accessibility
codes.definition: Data can no longer serve its intended use by authorised processes. Use A when it is unknown or irrelevant whether the data is gone (Av) or present but unusable (Ac).

codes.name: Unavailable state
codes.definition: Data is gone or unreachable — the resource no longer exists or cannot be technically reached by the infrastructure (deletion, wiper, storage loss, system offline).

codes.name: Inaccessible state
codes.definition: Data is present and reachable but cannot be used for its intended purpose by authorised processes (ransomware encryption, corruption of the container, permission lockout).

cause_side_partition.description: The partition of the cause side of any risk event into four rows by three questions asked in strict order. Exactly one row — Attack — is in TLCTC scope; the ten clusters classify its steps and only its steps (R-SCOPE). The other three rows are operational risk with no cluster. The partition is a property of the action, not of the actor (Axiom IV): the same person can produce events in different rows on the same day.
questions: Did the actor intend the outcome?
Did an accountable grantor confer an entitlement covering this action?

rows.name: Failure / external event
rows.definition: No actor. Software or hardware failure, misconfiguration without intent, capacity exhaustion without an attacker, or an external event. At the system altitude this is a System Failure, one of the system-altitude events outside the clusters' reach (system_risk_event.other_system_altitude_events).

rows.name: Error in Use
rows.definition: An actor, any actor, acting without intending the outcome. Entitlement is not asked: a visitor who trips a breaker is Error in Use, not #8. Can enter any altitude directly and can produce any Data Risk Event type (a misdirected email is C, an accidental purge is Av).

rows.name: Abuse of Rights
rows.definition: An actor acting intentionally inside an entitlement — an access right, a role, a mandate — genuinely conferred by an accountable grantor, but against its purpose. The envelope — its objects, actions and limits — is honoured and the system behaved as designed and as authorised, so there is no generic vulnerability, no cluster and no System Risk Event; the consequence chain begins at the Data Risk Event. Examples: a badge holder propping open a door, an administrator using genuine root to exfiltrate, a clerk posting a false entry inside their role, an officer approving a payment inside their mandate, a claims handler knowingly approving an inflated claim inside their approval limit. Answered by segregation of duties, four-eyes, mandate limits, supervision, vetting and purpose auditing — owned by the CRO, the business line and HR, not the CISO.

rows.name: Attack
rows.definition: An actor acting intentionally with no entitlement covering the action — an outsider with no grant, or an insider reaching past the envelope they were granted. The ten TLCTC clusters classify every step (exactly one per step, Axiom VI) and a System Compromise is recorded. A stolen entitlement is never Abuse of Rights: the grant attaches to the person, not the token, so credential use by a non-grantee is #4 (R-CRED) and the functions reached with it are #1.

entitlement.definition: What an accountable grantor actually conferred on a person for an action: an access right, a role, or a mandate, held genuinely. Its envelope is scope — the objects, the actions, and the limits (quantity, value, time, frequency) the grant covers. Purpose is not part of the envelope: it is the conduct norm the grant is given for. An in-envelope action for its purpose is legitimate use, an in-envelope action against it is Abuse of Rights, and purpose never widens or narrows the envelope.
entitlement.entitled_not_permitted: Permission is what the access-control system happens to return; entitlement is what a grantor conferred. The two are supposed to coincide and frequently do not; that gap is where the classification of a technical act depends on a governance document, and the framework refuses to pretend a question about authorization can be answered without consulting the authority.
entitlement.attaches_to_person_not_token: An entitlement is conferred on a grantee, never on a credential. An attacker holding the artifact was never a grantee, so no action they take is inside any envelope, however closely it mirrors what the grantee could have done.
entitlement.asymmetry_with_cluster_1: #1 Abuse of Functions reaches past the entitlement using functions the designer left open; its generic vulnerability is reducible by design (narrow the API, tighten the scope). Abuse of Rights uses the entitlement as given, for a purpose the grantor did not intend; a granted entitlement is irreducible by design. Two exposures, two levers, two owners, two registers.

cause_side_partition.third_party_modifier: Third party is a modifier, not a fifth row: any of the four rows may occur in another responsibility sphere and be honoured across a trust boundary. The notation already carries the modifier as the domain-boundary operator ||[ctx][@A->@B]||. #10 Supply Chain Attack is only the Attack-row instance of it at the system altitude; a supplier's outage honoured across the boundary is third-party failure, not #10.
decision_procedure: 1. Is there an actor? No -> Failure / external event. Operational risk. No cluster.
2. Did the actor intend the outcome? No -> Error in Use. Operational risk. No cluster.
3. Did an accountable grantor confer an entitlement covering THIS action? Yes -> Abuse of Rights. Operational risk. No SRE; the chain starts at the DRE. No -> continue.

4. Otherwise -> classify under the cluster rules. Cyber; SRE recorded. For example: an implementation flaw was required -> #2 / #3 per R-ROLE; a designed function was used outside the envelope -> #1 Abuse of Functions. (R-CRED, R-EXEC, R-SPECIFIC, R-SUPPLY and the others apply to this and every later step unchanged.)

system_risk_event.definition: Any risk event at the system altitude: the point at which a system's behaviour, privileges, data, or trust relationships depart from what its owner controls. The SRE is the central event of the Cyber Bow-Tie and the first node of the consequence chain SRE -> DRE -> BRE*. The SRE the framework defines is System Compromise, reached only through cluster steps; every cluster step records one, so a path of n cluster steps records n SREs, each admitting a Data Risk Event, a further cluster step (a chained SRE, against the same system or another), or both. Other events occur at the same altitude that serve no attacker's objective - System Failure is the standing example - and are operational risk with no cluster; the framework names them to place the boundary, not to classify them. Classification applies to steps that succeeded: a cluster assignment asserts the step's SRE, and an attempted or blocked step records no SRE and is not a step of an attack path.

types.name: System Compromise — Loss of Control
types.definition: The behaviour, privileges, data, or trust relationships of a system — or of a communication relationship it takes part in — are brought outside what their owner controls, in service of an attacker's objective. Reached only through cluster steps (the Attack row). This is the pivot of the Cyber Bow-Tie: everything the ten clusters classify converges on it, and the detection-and-intervention window between compromise and any Data Risk Event exists only for this type.

other_system_altitude_events.description: Events at the same altitude as System Compromise that serve no attacker's objective. Operational risk; no cluster; same conditional gate ("only if data is affected") into the data layer, so they share the consequence chain while having no cause-side classification. Named to place the boundary of the ten clusters, not to classify what lies outside it.

examples.name: System Failure — Loss of Function
examples.definition: The system ceases to perform its function and no attacker's objective is served: software or hardware failure, misconfiguration, capacity exhaustion without an attacker, an external event, or an unintended act (Error in Use) that breaks the system. Operational risk; no cluster. It sits at the same altitude as Compromise and passes through the same conditional gate ('only if data is affected') into the data layer, so it shares the consequence chain while having no cause-side classification.

system_risk_event.notes: v2.5 widening (2026-09-05): earlier v2.5 text defined the SRE as the attacker's loss-of-control event only; System Failure, drawn at the same altitude in the framework's figures without being defined, was named as a second type. v2.5 re-centering (2026-09-10): that gave Failure a co-equal standing the figures never showed and the clusters never reach. The SRE the framework defines is System Compromise alone; System Failure is retained verbatim as the standing example of other system-altitude events, moved from `types` to `other_system_altitude_events`. The definition now also states the per-step rule the prose had already adopted: every cluster step records an SRE. Abuse of Rights produces no SRE at all: the system was obeyed, not compromised, and did not fail; its chain begins at the DRE (R-SCOPE). v2.6 (C12, C13): the Compromise definition is restated around behaviour leaving owner control rather than an actor holding capability, so that a flood (a service's capacity taken out of its owner's control) and passive interception (a communication relationship taken out of it) meet the definition without special pleading; and the success-only scope is stated: an attempted or blocked step records no SRE and is not classified as a path step.

changes_from_v2_5.review_point: 1 — partition does not follow one principle
changes_from_v2_5.summary: Derivation restated as an analytical decomposition under a stated criterion (a distinct control lever and owner per generic vulnerability); #1 and #2/#3 named as residual clusters; exclusivity credited to R-SPECIFIC and the boundary tests.
R-FLOOD, R-CHANNEL and R-SUBSTRATE folded into R-SPECIFIC (capacity, channel, substrate clauses, propositions unchanged); the three IDs are retired aliases; registry 19 -> 17.
#10 definition amended to name subversion of the trusted third party, aligning it with the cluster's own generic vulnerability (Axioms VI/VII).
Subversion test and reworded falsifier: #10 requires a subverted trust artifact or issuer; a flaw in a legitimately supplied component is classified where it is exploited (Log4Shell #2).

Federation rewritten: credential or assertion presentation is #4 wherever presented; SP acceptance of a non-subverted IdP assertion is not a step; #10 -> #4 only where the IdP or its trust material was subverted.
R-SUPPLY gains the subversion requirement; thought-experiment step 10 names subversion.
The envelope is scope (objects, actions, limits); purpose is the conduct norm separating Abuse of Rights from legitimate use and never widens or narrows the envelope.
Adoboli removed from the canon; replaced by a claims-handler pair (inside the limit, inflated claim: Abuse of Rights [DRE: Ii]; over an unenforced limit: #1).

The data-vs-code boundary enters the dictionary (fec) and core #7: FEC is content run by a general-purpose engine; domain-specific expression languages are data unless they reach one.

changes_from_v2_5.review_point: 5 — publish a position on prompt injection
changes_from_v2_5.summary: Prompt injection, jailbreaks, context poisoning and agent tool abuse are #1; #1 -> #7 where the agent executes attacker-controlled code; the agent is the capability vector, not the actor.

changes_from_v2_5.summary: System Compromise restated around behaviour, privileges, data or trust relationships of a system or communication relationship leaving owner control in service of an attacker, covering floods and passive interception.
Successes only: a cluster assignment asserts the step's SRE; attempts are indicators, not path steps; stated as a scope limit.
